newsitem.title: USA: Wis. lawmakers to struggle with school funding.
newsitem.headline: Wis. lawmakers to struggle with school funding.

text.p: Wisconsin lawmakers will face a tough budget session that will include maintaining the state's committment to fund two-thirds of the costs of primary and secondary public schools, according to state officials.

Dave Mancl, chief of staff to House Speaker Ben Brancel, R-Endeavor, said continuing to maintain the two-thirds funding level in the fiscal 1998-99 bienium will be the driving force behind budget deliberations.

In fiscal 1997, which began July 1, the state reached the two-thirds funding level, allocating nearly $3.2 billion in general state aid to schools, according to the Wisconsin Legislative Fiscal Bureau.

Senate Majority Leader Chuck Cvala, D-Madison, agreed that maintaining the school funding level will be an important issue, given that revenue growth is not projected to be as strong as in past years.
Other matters to come up before lawmakers include greater funding for prisons and the state's ambitious welfare reform program, Cvala said.

The legislature is also expected to take up transportation funding in the wake of a December Legislative Audit Bureau Report that identified $2.9 billion of highway rehabilitation needs and expansion projects and warned that debt service payments on bonds sold to fund major transportation projects will exceed the amount of proceeds from future debt issuance by the turn of the century.
As the new speaker of the House, Brancel plans to create a new land-use committee to examine how land, particularly farmland, is taxed, Mancl said.

Another hot issue for lawmakers may be the state's lottery tax credit for homeowners, which was ruled unconstitutional by state courts because it excludes owners of vacation homes. Mancl said that lawmakers may want to wait until the appeal process in the lawsuit is exhausted before working on the tax credit law.
Lawmakers are scheduled to get down to business on Jan. 28, according to Cvala.
